verdicts.text: SST (Serverless Stack) originally started with AWS CDK.
verdicts.evidence: SST's own `packages/sst/package.json` at tag v2.0.0 lists `"aws-cdk":"2.62.2","aws-cdk-lib":"2.62.2"` and `"constructs":"10.1.156"` as dependencies, so the pre-Pulumi SST releases were built on AWS CDK. I didn't check the v0/v1 tags, so "originally" is supported by this release rather than confirmed back to the first version.

verdicts.text: Debugging with AWS CDK was frustrating due to CloudFormation templates.
verdicts.evidence: (escalated from pass1) SST's own post about its move lists debugging problems caused by the CDK/CloudFormation deployment model: "This can be really hard to debug because it's not immediately apparent what's going on." It also says CDK is "a JSON generator" that can "generate JSON CloudFormation templates that won't work."
verdicts.framing_note: This is an editorial paraphrase of SST's complaints. The source calls one specific CDK/CFN scenario "really hard to debug," while the claim turns that into a general statement that "debugging was frustrating due to CloudFormation templates." It's a loose summary, but it reflects the source fairly.

verdicts.text: Multi-cloud deployment was nearly impossible with AWS CDK.
verdicts.evidence: (escalated from pass1) AWS CDK compiles to CloudFormation and only works with AWS. Independent sources back up the Pulumi post's wording: Fively says Pulumi opened up "integrations previously unavailable in the older versions that relied solely on AWS CDK", and SST's v3 migration docs say Pulumi providers "allow you to build on any cloud". "Nearly impossible" is a subjective way of saying it, but it fits CDK being AWS-only.
verdicts.source: https://sst.dev/docs/migrate-from-v2/ ; https://5ly.co/blog/sst3-switching-to-ion/ ; WebSearch ran query "SST moving away from CDK Pulumi Terraform multi-cloud"
verdicts.intuition_flag: This is an editorial opinion. It's accurate in spirit because CDK is AWS-only, but SST's own "Moving away from CDK" post mostly blames CloudFormation's design, not multi-cloud limits.

verdicts.text: SST moved from AWS CDK to Pulumi.
verdicts.evidence: SST's current v3 engine (module `github.com/sst/sst/v3`) depends directly on `github.com/pulumi/pulumi/pkg/v3 v3.215.0` and `github.com/pulumi/pulumi/sdk/v3 v3.215.0`, and its go.mod has no AWS CDK dependency. That fits the claim that SST moved from its earlier CDK base to Pulumi.
verdicts.framing_note: This is indirect evidence. The v3 dependency on Pulumi is confirmed, but I didn't fetch an SST announcement or the v2 CDK code to show the earlier CDK base. SST v3 also uses Terraform providers through Pulumi bridging, which the claim leaves out.

verdicts.text: Pulumi lets SST offer a provider-agnostic infrastructure experience.
verdicts.evidence: (escalated from pass1) SST's own post on moving off CDK says it built its deployment around "the Pulumi deployment engine and their bridged Terraform providers." A separate third-party writeup says SST on Pulumi "now supports all of the Pulumi packages" and can link resources across different cloud providers. Together these back the characterization that Pulumi gives SST a provider-agnostic setup.
verdicts.framing_note: No source is cited in the claim. It's a loose summary sentence ("provider-agnostic experience"), and independent sources back it. The live pulumi.com copy of the post under review wasn't used as evidence.

verdicts.text: SST was originally built on top of AWS's Cloud Development Kit (CDK).
verdicts.evidence: SST v2's core package (sst/v2 packages/sst/package.json, version 2.49.8) depends on "aws-cdk-lib": "2.224.0", "constructs": "10.3.0", "@aws-cdk/cx-api" and "@aws-cdk/toolkit-lib", so the pre-Pulumi SST really was built on AWS CDK. (The blog post itself isn't counted as evidence.)

verdicts.text: AWS CDK allows developers to define their infrastructure using TypeScript or Python.
verdicts.evidence: (escalated from pass1) The AWS CDK v2 guide says CDK "has first-class support for the TypeScript, JavaScript, Python, Java, C#, and Go general-purpose programming languages." That confirms TypeScript and Python are both supported. The claim is true, but it is incomplete because it names only two of the six supported languages.
verdicts.intuition_flag: Readers could take "TypeScript or Python" to mean those are the only two options. CDK also supports JavaScript, Java, C#, and Go, so the wording may understate CDK's language support in a CDK-vs-Pulumi comparison.

verdicts.text: With AWS CDK and CloudFormation, the infrastructure code is a code generator that produces an intermediary format (such as YAML or JSON) that is executed to deploy resources.
verdicts.evidence: Pulumi's CDK comparison page backs this up: "running `cdk synth` produces an AWS Cloud Assembly — CloudFormation JSON or YAML templates plus other deployment assets — which is uploaded to Amazon S3/ECR and deployed by the AWS CloudFormation service." One small imprecision: plain CloudFormation templates are written by hand, not generated. The code-generator description really fits CDK, the part of the "CDK and CloudFormation" pairing that produces the templates.
verdicts.framing_note: The claim's link points to the CloudFormation comparison anchor, and the CDK comparison page describes the same synth-to-template model the claim describes.

verdicts.text: AWS CDK is AWS-centric.
verdicts.evidence: The linked comparison page (#what-is-aws-cdk) says CDK is "an AWS-maintained framework... for defining AWS infrastructure" and that "CDK is AWS-only." CDK synthesizes CloudFormation templates, and the AWS CloudFormation service deploys them. That is well-established public fact.
verdicts.framing_note: The source says 'CDK is AWS-only' and the claim says 'AWS-centric', so the source's stronger statement covers the claim.

verdicts.text: CloudFormation is AWS-centric.
verdicts.evidence: CloudFormation is AWS's own managed service for provisioning AWS resources. The Pulumi comparison page backs this up: "CloudFormation is AWS-only; third-party resources are supported through CloudFormation Registry extensions". Calling it "AWS-centric" is accurate, and softer than "AWS-only" because it allows for those Registry extensions.
verdicts.framing_note: The blog's inline link on L97 points to the AWS CDK comparison page, not the CloudFormation one. The claim is a well-known general fact, and a Pulumi docs page supports it, but that page is not an independent AWS source.

verdicts.text: Pulumi supports AWS, Azure, GCP, and on-premises infrastructure.
verdicts.evidence: The Pulumi IaC docs say "Manage infrastructure across AWS, Azure, Google Cloud, Kubernetes, and thousands of cloud providers". For on-premises, Pulumi ships first-party providers such as pulumi/pulumi-vsphere: "A Pulumi resource package for VMWare VSphere, providing multi-language access to vCenter Server and ESXi."

verdicts.text: Pulumi provides real-time debugging.
verdicts.evidence: The auto-generated `pulumi up` CLI reference lists `--attach-debugger`: "Enable the ability to attach a debugger to the program and source based plugins being executed." That supports live debugging of the program while a deployment is running. "Real-time debugging" is vague comparison-table marketing wording, but the underlying capability exists.
verdicts.intuition_flag: "Real-time debugging" is loose marketing language; the closest concrete feature is --attach-debugger / --debug output.

verdicts.text: Pulumi supports any programming language.
verdicts.evidence: Pulumi supports a fixed set of languages, not "any" language. The product repo's sdk/README.md says it "contains Pulumi SDKs for the following languages", and the Languages & SDKs docs page says: "Pulumi supports TypeScript, JavaScript, Python, Go, .NET, Java, YAML, and HCL." Adding a new language is possible, but it takes a custom language host ("it's possible to add your own language").
verdicts.source: gh search code --repo pulumi/pulumi --filename README.md Languages (sdk/README.md); repo:content/docs/iac/languages-sdks/_index.md L9, L55
verdicts.framing_note: Overclaim: "Any programming language" in the comparison table vs. a listed set of 8 supported languages. Suggest "TypeScript, Python, Go, C#, Java, YAML, and more".
verdicts.intuition_flag: The same table row says AWS CDK supports only "TypeScript, Python", but CDK also supports Java, C#, and Go, so the row is skewed on both sides.

verdicts.text: Pulumi provides clear deployment state visibility.
verdicts.evidence: The docs show Pulumi keeps explicit, inspectable deployment state: "The `pulumi stack export` and `pulumi stack import` commands can be used to export the latest or a specific version of a stack's state. This can be used to inspect or even manually edit the contents". They also say the state file uses "a relatively easy to understand JSON format", and preview/refresh compare recorded state against the program. "Clear" is a subjective marketing word, so the capability behind the claim checks out but the adjective can't be verified.
verdicts.intuition_flag: This is a subjective marketing line in a comparison table ("Clear deployment state"), not a precise, falsifiable feature claim.

verdicts.text: Pulumi supports custom providers and workflows for extensibility.
verdicts.evidence: The Pulumi docs describe dynamic providers as lighter weight than custom providers, and point to bridged or native providers for more complex APIs. Dynamic providers exist for cases where "You want to create some new custom resource types." That confirms the custom-provider half of the claim. The "workflows" half is too vague to check against a specific source, but it is harmless.
verdicts.intuition_flag: "workflows for extensibility" is marketing language with no checkable meaning.

verdicts.text: Pulumi treats infrastructure code as a first-class program executed directly during deployment, rather than generating an intermediary format.
verdicts.evidence: Pulumi's architecture guide says that during `pulumi up`, "the Pulumi CLI launches the ... language host and requests that it execute the program," and that the language host sends resource registration requests to the engine while it keeps running. The program itself runs at deploy time, and the engine works on those registrations with no generated template (such as CloudFormation) in between.
verdicts.framing_note: The docs describe the program running directly. The "no intermediary format" part is an inference from how the engine consumes registrations over RPC; the guide doesn't say it outright.

verdicts.text: With Pulumi, the infrastructure code is the same code that runs during deployment.
verdicts.evidence: Pulumi's architecture guide backs this up: on `pulumi up`, "the Pulumi CLI launches the ... language host and requests that it execute the program", and "The language host continues to execute your program concurrently with the engine processing this request". So the user's program itself runs while the deployment happens, rather than being turned into an intermediate template first.
verdicts.framing_note: This is a general statement about Pulumi's execution model. The only evidence is a Pulumi docs page, which can confirm the claim but isn't product source, so confidence is medium.

verdicts.text: Pulumi's provider-agnostic approach allows SST's team to work with a wide range of cloud and on-premises platforms.
verdicts.evidence: Pulumi publishes providers for many public clouds and for on-prem platforms too. For example, pulumi/pulumi-vsphere is described as "A Pulumi resource package for VMWare VSphere, providing multi-language access to vCenter Server and ESXi". The part about SST's team is a general description with nothing specific to check against a source.
verdicts.framing_note: The line in the post says "easily work with", but the extracted claim leaves out "easily". The claim is a general capability statement.

verdicts.text: The Founding Engineer at SST said: "With Pulumi, the deployment process feels like a natural extension of writing code - it's intuitive and powerful and capable of advanced things that traditional IaC tools can't handle."
verdicts.evidence: I couldn't find this quote anywhere except the blog post being reviewed, and that post can't serve as its own evidence. The PulumiUP 2024 page confirms that Dax Raad is SST's Founding Engineer and gave the talk "From CDK to Pulumi: Evolution of SST". So the quote may come from that talk, but I found no transcript or other outside record of these words.
verdicts.source: WebSearch ran query "\"natural extension of writing code\" Pulumi SST intuitive and powerful"; only the reviewed page (pulumi.com/blog/aws-cdk-vs-pulumi-why-sst-switched/) came up. Speaker attribution came from https://www.pulumi.com/blog/pulumiup-global-cloud-iac-platform-engineering-ai-conference/
verdicts.framing_note: The quote is credited to a role (SST Founding Engineer), not to a checkable document; no outside source was found.
verdicts.intuition_flag: The wording is polished and marketing-style ("intuitive and powerful and capable of advanced things"), so it could be a paraphrase. The author should confirm it word-for-word against the PulumiUP talk recording and consider naming the speaker (Dax Raad).

verdicts.text: Pulumi provides improved visibility and debugging capabilities as described at https://www.pulumi.com/product/pulumi-insights/.
verdicts.evidence: (escalated from pass1) Pulumi's own materials back up the "visibility" part: the Insights docs say it "provides comprehensive cloud visibility and policy enforcement", and the concepts page describes "advanced search, analytics, and AI for your infrastructure as code". None of the results present Insights as a debugging tool. The cited /product/pulumi-insights/ page did not come up in search, so I couldn't check its current text or whether the URL is still live.
verdicts.source: https://www.pulumi.com/docs/insights/ ; https://www.pulumi.com/docs/insights/concepts/ ; WebSearch ran query "Pulumi Insights product page"
verdicts.framing_note: overclaim: the sources describe 'cloud visibility', 'search, analytics, and AI'; the claim adds 'debugging capabilities', which the sources don't support
verdicts.intuition_flag: In a CDK-vs-Pulumi migration post, 'debugging' likely means deployment debugging, which Insights (resource search/discovery/policy) doesn't do. Also confirm that /product/pulumi-insights/ still resolves and doesn't redirect to Insights & Governance or a waitlist page.

verdicts.text: Pulumi has built-in extensibility features such as custom providers and dynamic components.
verdicts.evidence: Pulumi's docs describe custom providers, "dynamic providers in TypeScript and Python, which let you declare custom resources inline", and separately component resources ("a logical grouping of other resources"). There is no Pulumi feature called "dynamic components". The claim mixes up dynamic providers and component resources.
verdicts.framing_note: shifted: the docs name "dynamic providers" and "component resources", but the claim invents "dynamic components". The overall point (Pulumi is extensible, including through custom providers) is accurate.
verdicts.intuition_flag: "Dynamic components" is not a Pulumi term. It should probably read "dynamic providers" or "component resources".

verdicts.text: SST's Pulumi-based foundation is in place, allowing the SST team to focus on further enhancing developer experience.
verdicts.evidence: (escalated from pass1) SST's own v3 announcement confirms the Pulumi-based engine shipped: "Ion is now officially being released as SST v3," built on "a new deployment engine that would use Pulumi and Terraform." The second half of the claim, that this lets the team focus on developer experience, is the author's own characterization. No source states it outright.
verdicts.framing_note: The source confirms that the Pulumi-based foundation shipped as SST v3 (Aug 2024). The claim's focus on developer experience is the author's reading, not a statement from SST.

verdicts.text: Pulumi supports more advanced deployment workflows as described at https://www.pulumi.com/docs/pulumi-cloud/deployments/.
verdicts.evidence: The linked docs cover Pulumi Deployments. The section index (content/docs/deployments/_index.md) says: "Cloud-hosted deployment automation, drift detection, and workflow management for infrastructure as code." The line itself is mostly about what SST plans to do. Its only checkable part is that Pulumi offers deployment workflow features, and the docs confirm that.
verdicts.framing_note: The docs describe "deployment automation ... and workflow management". The blog says Pulumi can support "more advanced deployment workflows", which is a loose, promotional way of saying the same thing.
verdicts.intuition_flag: The docs have moved to /docs/deployments/. I couldn't find an alias for the exact /docs/pulumi-cloud/deployments/ root, only for subpaths like get-started. Check that the link still redirects.

verdicts.text: Pulumi Crosswalk for AWS simplifies "day one" tasks, as described in the AWS guide at /docs/iac/guides/clouds/aws/.
verdicts.evidence: The linked AWS guide never mentions "Crosswalk" or "day one". Old /docs/reference/crosswalk/ URLs now redirect to it as aliases, and it describes AWSx as "higher-level components that implement well-architected patterns for common AWS services". The link resolves, but it no longer supports the "Crosswalk simplifies day one tasks" wording.
verdicts.framing_note: shifted: the claim calls the target a Crosswalk "day one" guide, but the page is a general AWS guides index (AWS provider, AWSx, EKS, etc.) with no Crosswalk branding.
verdicts.intuition_flag: The "Crosswalk for AWS" name looks retired from the docs (its old URLs are now aliases), so the link text is stale.

verdicts.text: There is an on-demand workshop titled "Getting Started with Infrastructure as Code on AWS" available at https://www.pulumi.com/resources/getting-started-with-iac-pulumi-aws/.
verdicts.evidence: (escalated from pass1) A Pulumi workshop with exactly this title exists, but search only finds it at /events/getting-started-with-iac-pulumi-aws/, not at the cited /resources/ path. That page says "This workshop is designed to help new users become familiar with the core concepts needed to effectively deploy resources on AWS using Pulumi." I couldn't confirm that the /resources/ URL resolves or redirects there, or that the workshop is on-demand.
verdicts.framing_note: Title matches. The URL path differs (/resources/ in the claim vs /events/ in search results), and nothing found confirms the "on-demand" label.
verdicts.intuition_flag: The cited /resources/ path may be a legacy alias; check the frontmatter aliases on the events page in the pulumi/docs repo to confirm the link isn't broken.

verdicts.text: The blog post 'SST Runs on the Pulumi Engine: What It Means to Build on Pulumi' at /blog/sst-built-on-pulumi/ provides a closer look at the engine mechanics behind SST's migration to Pulumi.
verdicts.evidence: PR pulumi/docs#21651 adds the target page at content/blog/sst-built-on-pulumi/index.md, titled "SST Runs on the Pulumi Engine: What It Means to Build on Pulumi." That PR says the post covers "what 'built on the Pulumi engine' means mechanically." The same PR adds this cross-link to the conclusion of the 2024 post. The title, path and description all match.
verdicts.framing_note: The PR says the post covers "what 'built on the Pulumi engine' means mechanically"; the claim calls it "a closer look at the engine mechanics." These say the same thing.
verdicts.intuition_flag: The target page only exists once #21651 merges. Before that, pulumi.com/blog/sst-built-on-pulumi/ returned 404 (reported in #21673), so the link must ship in the same PR as the new post.

verdicts.text: SST is a framework that makes building modern full-stack applications on your infrastructure easy.
verdicts.evidence: This FAQ answer is a promotional one-line description of SST that paraphrases SST's own tagline (building full-stack apps on your own infrastructure). "Easy" is a subjective judgment, not a falsifiable fact. The factual core, that SST is a full-stack app framework, is uncontroversial and fits the surrounding content (L193–197) describing SST's Pulumi-based Ion engine.
verdicts.intuition_flag: Marketing tagline paraphrase; if you want strict checking, compare it with sst.dev's current homepage wording.

verdicts.text: SST's Ion is the code name for a new engine for deploying SST applications.
verdicts.evidence: SST's own blog says: "Ion is a code name for a new engine for deploying SST applications." A later SST v3 post confirms that Ion shipped as SST v3, so the "new engine" wording is historical but was accurate for its time.
verdicts.framing_note: Source says "Ion is a code name for a new engine for deploying SST applications"; the claim says "the code name", which is essentially the same statement.

verdicts.text: SST Ion's constructs (or components) are deployed using Pulumi instead of CDK and CloudFormation (CFN).
verdicts.evidence: SST's own announcement says: "The constructs (or components) are defined using Terraform providers and deployed using Pulumi; as opposed to CDK and CloudFormation (CFN)." The claim leaves out the "defined using Terraform providers" part, but what it does say is still correct.
verdicts.framing_note: The source says components are "defined using Terraform providers and deployed using Pulumi; as opposed to CDK and CFN". The claim keeps only the deployment half, which the source fully supports.

verdicts.text: SST leverages Pulumi behind the scenes for its providers and deployment engine.
verdicts.evidence: SST's official "What is SST" docs state: "SST uses Pulumi behind the scenes for the providers and the deployment engine."
verdicts.framing_note: The claim paraphrases SST's own docs sentence almost word for word ("uses" → "leverages").

verdicts.text: SST bridges Terraform providers through Pulumi.
verdicts.evidence: SST's own docs say "SST uses Pulumi behind the scenes for the providers and the deployment engine. And Terraform's providers are bridged through Pulumi."
verdicts.framing_note: Source: "Terraform's providers are bridged through Pulumi" (on SST's docs); claim: "SST bridges Terraform providers through Pulumi."

verdicts.text: SST primarily relies on SaaS revenue through its managed platform and potentially supplemental income streams like enterprise services and consulting.
verdicts.evidence: SST's docs show it charges for a managed SaaS product, the Console: "Starting Feb 1, 2025, the Console will be priced based on the number of active resources in your SST apps." That supports the existence of SaaS revenue. But SST doesn't publish how its revenue breaks down, and the company is venture-funded (seed round per Crunchbase), so "primarily relies" can't be checked. The "enterprise services and consulting" part is hedged speculation with no source.
verdicts.framing_note: Source confirms a paid Console exists; claim adds that SST "primarily relies" on it and guesses at other income, which no public source discloses.
verdicts.intuition_flag: The claim guesses at a private company's revenue mix ("potentially...") — consider rewording to "SST monetizes via its paid Console" instead.

verdicts.text: SST Console is optional and includes a free tier.
verdicts.evidence: SST's official Console docs state: "The Console is completely optional and comes with a free tier." The free tier currently covers workspaces with 350 or fewer active resources.
verdicts.framing_note: source: "completely optional and comes with a free tier" vs claim: "optional and includes a free tier"

verdicts.evidence: The line `date: 2026-09-16` is the blog post's own front matter publication date. It's metadata the PR author sets, not a factual claim that could be checked against an outside source.

verdicts.text: In SST's architecture, `sst deploy` reads the user's `sst.config.ts` and resolves SST's own components, which compile into Pulumi resource declarations, after which the Pulumi engine diffs desired vs. actual state, builds a dependency graph, and orders operations, then Terraform-bridged providers translate each resource into cloud API calls, and state is written to an S3 bucket in the user's AWS account.
verdicts.evidence: SST's docs and v3 announcement back up each step: SST v3 is a deployment engine that "would use Pulumi and Terraform", its AWS provider is "from Pulumi that's built on Terraform", and "the state is stored locally and backed up to S3 in your AWS account." One caveat: SST's config docs say the state is "generated locally and backed up in your cloud provider", and the home provider can be AWS, Cloudflare, or local. So S3 applies only when the home provider is AWS.
verdicts.framing_note: The claim describes the default AWS setup ("state is written to an S3 bucket"). SST's source is broader: state is "generated locally and backed up" to the home provider, which can be AWS, Cloudflare, or local. The claim also leaves out that state is generated locally first. The Pulumi engine's internals (diffing, dependency graph) are standard Pulumi behavior; SST's pages don't describe them.

verdicts.text: SST v3 replaced AWS CDK with an embedded Pulumi engine.
verdicts.evidence: SST's own source, platform/package.json in sst/sst, depends on "@pulumi/pulumi": "3.215.0" along with @pulumi/aws, @pulumi/cloudflare and other Pulumi providers. It has no aws-cdk dependency, which fits v3 moving off CDK onto Pulumi. The package.json doesn't show the "embedded engine" detail directly. That part comes from the SST blog quote the post cites ("an embedded Pulumi engine"), which I didn't fetch here.

verdicts.text: SST v3 replaced AWS CDK and CloudFormation with an embedded Pulumi engine that calls Terraform-bridged providers to make the underlying cloud API calls.
verdicts.evidence: SST's own blog says Ion (released as v3) builds components "defined using Terraform providers and deployed using Pulumi; as opposed to CDK and CloudFormation," and that SST uses "the Pulumi deployment engine and their bridged Terraform providers." It also says the providers "are basically calls to the AWS SDK," and that you only install the SST CLI with "nothing else to install," which fits the "embedded engine" wording.
verdicts.framing_note: The SST v3 post confirms "a new deployment engine that would use Pulumi and Terraform, as opposed to CDK and CloudFormation," which was released as v3.

verdicts.text: Nitric runs application deployments through the Pulumi engine rather than building its own diff, state, and provider layer from scratch.
verdicts.evidence: Nitric's docs say "All of the direct deployment providers use Pulumi under the hood for their deployments," and its pre-built providers use the Pulumi Automation API. Nitric also offers Terraform providers that generate IaC, and the claim does not mention them.
verdicts.framing_note: Source: the official/direct deployment providers use Pulumi (Terraform IaC-generating providers also exist). The claim that deployments run through the Pulumi engine holds for Nitric's default providers. The "rather than building its own layer" part is the author's reading, though it fits Nitric's "Why we started with Pulumi" post.

verdicts.text: SST's team's public attention has broadened to include opencode, but that hasn't changed SST's release cadence or its dependency on the Pulumi engine.
verdicts.evidence: SST kept shipping v4.x often in spring 2026: mise-versions shows "1253 releases over 6y (~2d avg)", with several releases a day in April–May 2026. But the GitHub releases page in the search results lists v4.17.0, released 26 Jun 2026, as "Latest". That leaves a possible three-month gap before today (Sept 28), so no source settles "cadence unchanged". It is well established that SST v3+ runs on the Pulumi engine, but I found no current source that confirms it, and "public attention has broadened" is an editorial judgment that can't be checked.
verdicts.source: https://github.com/sst/sst/releases; https://mise-versions.jdx.dev/tools/sst; WebSearch ran query "SST releases 2026 github sst/sst"
verdicts.intuition_flag: The releases page's "Latest" is v4.17.0 from 26 Jun 2026. If that snapshot is current, SST's cadence may actually have slowed, which would undercut "hasn't changed SST's release cadence". A reviewer should check recent sst/sst tags.

verdicts.text: SST keeps state in an S3 bucket in the user's own AWS account.
verdicts.evidence: (escalated from pass1) SST's official docs say "The state is stored in a file locally and backed up to a bucket in your AWS (or Cloudflare) account." The State page adds that this bucket is "typically named sst-state-<hash>" and is created in your home region.
verdicts.framing_note: Minor nuance: SST keeps a local state file and backs it up to the S3 bucket. For Cloudflare-home apps the bucket is in Cloudflare, not AWS. The claim is accurate in the AWS context.

verdicts.text: The SST team has repeatedly stated, since the Ion rewrite shipped, that SST's architecture is built on the Pulumi engine as described.
verdicts.evidence: SST's own "Moving away from CDK" post says `sst deploy` resources "make a call to an embedded Pulumi engine", and that "their engine is embedded in the Ion CLI." This confirms that SST itself says it is built on the Pulumi engine. I only fetched this one SST post, though, and it dates from January 2024, before Ion shipped as v3. So "repeatedly" and "since the Ion rewrite shipped" are not directly proven.
verdicts.framing_note: Source (Jan 2024, before v3 shipped): "embedded Pulumi engine". The claim adds "repeatedly, since the Ion rewrite shipped". The main fact matches, but the time frame and repetition are only supported indirectly.
verdicts.intuition_flag: "Repeatedly stated since shipping" is vague, and the one SST statement I found predates the release. Consider citing a current sst.dev docs page instead.

verdicts.text: `sst deploy` handles provisioning end to end.
verdicts.evidence: SST's docs present `deploy` as the single command for deploying an app ("When you're ready to deploy your app, you can use the deploy command."). A code-derived DeepWiki summary adds that it covers "the complete deployment pipeline from configuration building through Pulumi execution to state persistence."
verdicts.framing_note: 'End to end' is a loose summary. It is backed by the DeepWiki description of the full pipeline (build config, run Pulumi, persist state). DeepWiki is a secondary, code-derived source.

verdicts.text: SST is an open source TypeScript framework, from the team formerly known as Serverless Stack, for building and deploying full-stack applications to AWS and more than 150 other providers.

verdicts.text: The Pulumi engine diffs desired vs. actual state, builds a dependency graph, and orders operations.
verdicts.evidence: Pulumi's docs say "The deployment engine is responsible for computing the set of operations needed to drive the current state of your infrastructure into the desired state expressed by your program." Resource ordering follows the dependency graph built from explicit and implicit dependencies. One caveat: without `pulumi refresh`, the engine compares against the recorded stack state, not live cloud state.
verdicts.framing_note: The docs say the engine compares the "existing state from our previous run" against the desired state. The claim calls that "actual state", a loose paraphrase that Pulumi's own blog also uses ("compare the to-be model with the actual state").
verdicts.intuition_flag: "Actual state" really means the last-recorded stack state unless a refresh is run. Worth a wording tweak if precision matters.

verdicts.text: Terraform-bridged providers translate each resource into cloud API calls, and this is handled by Pulumi's Terraform bridge.

SST also has other home providers (for example, Cloudflare), which the claim doesn't mention.
verdicts.intuition_flag: True for SST's default AWS home. SST can also store state in Cloudflare (R2) when home is set to cloudflare, so "always S3" is slightly too broad.

verdicts.text: Pulumi's engine does not require a Pulumi account, a network call to Pulumi Cloud, or any Pulumi-hosted service to run.

verdicts.intuition_flag: "Any Pulumi-hosted service" may go too far: by default the CLI downloads provider plugins from get.pulumi.com and GitHub. You can work around this with pre-installed plugins or a custom plugin server, but it isn't zero-network out of the box.

verdicts.text: Pulumi's Automation API works the same way (without requiring a Pulumi account or Pulumi Cloud) for teams embedding Pulumi programs inside their own tools.

One caveat: Pulumi Cloud is the default, and the Automation API guide lists "A Pulumi access token" as a prerequisite, so running without Pulumi Cloud takes a DIY-backend setup.
verdicts.intuition_flag: "Works the same way" sounds like zero config, but Automation API defaults to Pulumi Cloud, and its guide requires an access token unless you set up a DIY backend. It also runs the Pulumi CLI underneath, so it isn't a fully self-contained embedded engine.
